title: Autonomous Frontier-Based Exploration with High-Level VLM Guidance | EECS at UC Berkeley
content: Autonomous Frontier-Based Exploration with High-Level VLM Guidance | EECS at UC Berkeley Autonomous Frontier-Based Exploration with High-Level VLM Guidance Aarush Aitha EECS Department, University of California, Berkeley Technical Report No. UCB/EECS-2025-172 August 25, 2025 http://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2025/EECS-2025-172.pdf Even though autonomous navigation and exploration of unknown environments is an important task in robotics that has been explored extensively, human-like exploration has remained out of reach. This task is vital for robotic exploration and mapping of dangerous environments such as old and dilapidated buildings which are falling apart and are hazardous to humans. With the recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), robotics tasks such as exploration become approachable via the generalizable knowledge of these models. In this work, we develop a novel exploration pipeline that delegates high-level strategic planning to a VLM while relying on a conventional robotics stack for low-level control. The system first identifies frontiers, which are the boundaries between mapped and unmapped territory. When multiple exploration paths are available, the robot constructs a multimodal prompt containing the current top-down occupancy map and visual imagery of the candidate frontiers. The VLM analyzes this holistic data to select the single most promising frontier, replacing simple geometric heuristics with contextual spatial reasoning. The effectiveness of this method is verified in simulation across six distinct indoor environments from the Matterport3D dataset. Our proposed pipeline demonstrates superior reliability and eciency compared to existing methods, improving final map coverage by up to 24% in complex environments. We also show partially successful results from transferring our algorithm to a physical hexapod robot in a real home environment. The proposed pipeline is extremely lightweight and transferable to any hardware modality, not requiring any model training or heavy computational tasks, and is easily transferable to any robot with access to RGB-D and odometry data, as well as a standard internet connection.
